blocks.text: Traumatic Brain Injury (TBI)

TBI is defined as an alteration in brain function, or other evidence of brain pathology, caused by an external force. TBI is a leading cause of death and permanent disability worldwide. Primary brain injury occurs at time of trauma (e.g., cortical contusions, brain lacerations, diffuse axonal injury) while secondary injury develops following the initial insult (brain edema, hypoxemia, ischemia due to elevated intracranial pressure). TBI is often associated with ophthalmic, ENT, dental and maxillofacial injuries.

History and/or clinical evidence of blunt or penetrating trauma to the head
Transient or sustained alteration in level of consciousness s
Other evidence of altered brain function i.e., seizures, amnesia, focal deficits
Clinical classification of TBI
Perform the Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) to assess clinical severity of TBI across care paths. (see below)
Report each component of GCS; Eye, Verbal, and Mo tor response, e.g., E4V4M5, not just the total score.
If a GCS component is untestable due to intubation, sedation, etc., record the reason.

Management of TBI
Prehospital and Lower-Level Health Facilities Interventions
Take important history from patients and relatives (AMPLE)
Apply the BLS trauma protocol and perform a rapid neurological assessment
Protect the C -spine stabilizes the neck with rigid neck collar/improvised alternative devices until the x-ray c-spine is done
Give oxygen therapy to all patients with O2 saturation <92% (rate of 4L/min)
Give IV normal saline infusion through large gauge cannula
Avoid SBP of <90 mmHg in adults and older children
Catheterize the bladder and ensure urine output above 30ml per hour
Refer all polytrauma or isolated TBI patients with GCS<13, to center capable of providing definitive care.
Referred patients should be accompanied by a competent adult during transport.
Inform the destination hospital (by phone or letter of referring to non-emergencies) of the impending transfer.
Note: Do not give dextrose infusion for resuscitation in TBI.
Referral hospital and higher-level Facilities Interventions
Follow the ATLS ABCD trauma protocol
Send for rapid non -contrast brain CT scan all moderate and severe TBI patients

blocks.text: Management of Blood Pressure
Maintain SBP at 100mmHg to ensure cerebral perfusion.
Management of Moderate and Severe TBI
Multidisciplinary approach is of paramount importance in TBI management.
Admit all moderate and severe TBI patients to ICU for neurocritical care management.

Neurosurgical Interventions for TBI

Refer for emergency neurosurgical evaluation all patients with epidural hematomas (EDH), subdural hematomas (SDH), cerebral contusions, or intracerebral hematomas (ICH) with significant mass effect to the brain.

blocks.text: Consider craniotomy and hematoma evacuation for EDH with estimated volume above 30CC and Subdural hematoma with thickness above10mm or midline shift above 5mm

blocks.text: A lower threshold for surgical intervention is recommended for posterior fossa mass lesions.
A formal craniotomy is necessary to perform adequate evacuation of intracranial mass lesions
Consider decompressive craniectomy to relieve ICP only when medical treatment of raised ICP has failed and benefits outweigh the risks for such a procedure.

blocks.text: Elevate depressed skull fractures where surgical approach is indicated:
Open depressed fractures, gross contamination to prevent infection,
Low bleeding risk, e.g., no risk of dural venous sinus lacerations.
Exoscope Cistern ostomy.
Note: Depressed skull fracture over the sagittal sinus SHOULD NOT be treated surgically because of the high risk of uncontrollable hemorrhage
Extracranial Surgical Interventions
Delay non emergent extracranial surgical interventions in TBI patients unless they are life- saving procedures.
Orthopedic operations should ideally be delayed 24 -48 hours to allow initial stabilization of ICP
Consider damage control orthopedics with initial external fixation and later definitive treatment to minimize the risk for “second hit “phenomenon
